Another Whig Victory. The Vermont elections have resulted in the triumph of the Whigs. Their nomination for Governor, Lieutenant Governor, majority of the State Legislature, and every member of Congress, save one, have been successful. Majorities not yet ascertained.

Rhode Island.—The Whig Convention of Rhode Island, admitting the hopelessness of Mr. Clusters canse, have nominated Gen. Harrison as their candidate for the Presidency, and they express the strongest confidence of giving him the vote of the State.

Important from Spain.—Lisbon dates to the 13th ult. are received at Boston. Disturbances, which threatened the complete overthrow of the Queen's government, have broken out in parts of Spain heretofore well affected to her cause. The constitution of 1832, has been proclaimed at Cadiz, Seville, Badajoz and Malaga, and Madrid was in a state of insurrection. Without foreign interposition, Spain must become prey to anarchy.—Gen. Evans, the commander of the English Legion, had died.

Educated from his earliest infancy under the immediate superintendent of one of France's noblest and gentlest daughters, MADAME DE GENLIS, he could not be otherwise than generous and just. Secluded in the early stage of manhood from the corrupting influence of dissipated and intriguing courtiers, and having been constantly taught to look upon them with contempt, he could not but have imbibed the purest principles of republicanism. His peaceful and prosperous reign, and his violent and untimely death, will fill the brightest and the blackest page in the history of the civilized world.

The city is yet quiet—the national guards are under arms and patrolling the streets—the ministers, nominally at least, are in possession of power; and we understand, that the Due de Broglie has expressed his intention to call an early meeting of the chambers.—This is the course we should by all means recommend. And, in the mean time, we advise as those who have the welfare and honor of France at heart, to preserve tranquility until the ultimate decision of the chambers shall be known.

It is recommended, as will be seen by the general orders of the commander-in-chief, MARSHAL CLAUSEL, that the theatres, museums, les jardins, and all other public amusements and resorts be suspended for the space of six days; that the churches, generally, be opened for service during the same time; and that the citizens be requested to wear a badge of mourning on the left arm; which are in addition to the orders directed expressly to the national guards.

The usurper has fallen! Louis Philippe is dead. We do not lament his fall, though we could have wished him a more glorious end. He was shot yesterday on his way to the Boulevards, in his riding-side, and expired few hours afterwards. What is to be done? The people are yet quiet. The national guards are under arms; and power for the moment is in the hands of the ministers. This state of things cannot continue many hours. What the result will be, no one can anticipate.
